Title:JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.

report.summary: JANUS introduces a co-evolving world model that predicts and verifies research ideas, improving long-horizon autonomous scientific discovery efficiency and ceiling.
report.background: Autonomous research agents typically follow a Generate-Execute-Feedback loop: they propose hypotheses, run experiments, and update from results. This reactive trial-and-error is bottlenecked by expensive, slow executions, creating feedback delays while the search space explodes. JANUS, submitted to arXiv in October 2026, replaces blind execution with a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop. A co-evolving world model forecasts candidate outcomes before they run, while past experience is distilled into reusable skills. The work sits at the intersection of LLM agents, automated scientific discovery, model-based reinforcement learning, and graph-based search, aiming to make long-horizon research more sample-efficient and less dependent on costly real-world execution.
key_points: JANUS uses a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop. In an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates, and a world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility. It then selects, refines, or prunes branches before execution, reducing wasted experiments and focusing compute on the most promising research directions.

After ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for the research agent, exploration-strategy skills for the world model, and coordination protocols between them. This turns each execution into reusable knowledge rather than a one-off trial, supporting longer research horizons.

The research agent and world model co-evolve. The agent improves candidate generation, while the world model improves its predictive judgment over extended horizons. This mutual refinement aims to overcome the feedback-delay bottleneck that throttles conventional autonomous research systems.

Experiments on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks show JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. It achieves both higher evolving efficiency and a higher ceiling, suggesting that predictive world models plus skill distillation can make autonomous research agents more effective.
report.impact: For the AI industry, JANUS points toward a shift from reactive trial-and-error agents to predictive, model-based research systems. That could lower the compute and time cost of automated discovery, making autonomous labs more practical. Developers should watch techniques like co-evolving world models, graph-based candidate pruning, and skill distillation; these are transferable to coding agents, robotics, and enterprise workflow automation. For regular users, the payoff is faster scientific and technical progress, potentially better AI research assistants, and earlier access to validated findings. Risks include over-reliance on learned forecasts, benchmark overfitting, and hidden verification costs, so real-world validation remains essential.
report.tools: Related open-source projects to watch include AI-Scientist, Agent Laboratory, AutoGen, LangGraph, Voyager, and DreamerV3-style world models. MLS-Bench-Lite may serve as an evaluation starting point. Check the JANUS arXiv page for code or data releases, and follow arXiv cs.AI and Papers with Code for implementations. Combining graph-based agent frameworks with model-based RL tooling is the most direct way to experiment.
